opus-5.5.text:
I think the "super app" framing is understandable, but it's borrowed from the mobile internet era, and it may not fit very well.

In the mobile era, the logic was about traffic and entry points. Whoever owned the most daily active users and the most time spent could expand into payments, e-commerce, services, and so on. So people look at chatbots and think: this is the new entry point, so whoever wins the chatbot wins the super app. There's some truth to that. A chat interface is very general, and users do form habits around one product.

But I think the core competition is really about **model capability**, not the app. The chatbot is just the first form factor that made the capability visible to ordinary people. If one model becomes clearly better at reasoning, coding, or getting real work done, users move quite quickly. Switching costs are much lower than with a social network, because a chatbot doesn't have strong network effects. Your friends aren't locked inside it.

Also, I don't think chat is the final form. Right now most usage is: you ask a question, it gives you an answer. More and more value will come from the model actually doing things: writing and running code, operating software, completing long multi-step tasks. In that world, the important question isn't "which app do I open every day," but "which system can I trust to finish this task for me." That could live inside a chatbot, inside an IDE, inside an operating system, or behind an API that you never see directly.

So my view is that the chatbot competition is real and matters, especially for gathering user feedback and revenue to fund research. But treating it purely as a fight for a super app can mislead people into optimizing for distribution, features, and growth tricks, when the thing that really decides the long-term outcome is whether your model keeps getting meaningfully smarter. The app is a consequence; the intelligence is the cause.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities may move beyond chat and live in tools such as an IDE or operating system, but it does not raise the possibility that a differently formed future super app could subsume chatbot functionality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "super app" is a bit of a misleading frame, honestly. It borrows a mental model from the mobile internet era, where the game was about capturing attention and traffic, bundling as many services as possible into one entry point, and then monetizing the funnel. WeChat is the classic example. But a chatbot isn't fundamentally a traffic product. What you're really competing on is capability, and capability compounds in a very different way than user acquisition does.

Let me put it this way. In the app era, the product was mostly fixed, and the competition was about distribution. Whoever got to a billion users first won, because the marginal cost of serving the next user was near zero and network effects locked people in. With language models, the product itself is still changing every few months. A model that's meaningfully smarter, or that can actually complete a multi-step task for you instead of just answering a question, makes the previous one look obsolete. So the moat from having a lot of chatbot users is much thinner than people assume. Users will switch if something is noticeably better, and the switching cost is close to zero because there's no social graph, no accumulated content, nothing that really anchors you.

Now, there is a version of the super app argument that I think has some truth to it. If you think about where things are heading, the chat interface is probably a transitional form. What people actually want isn't to chat, it's to get things done. And the moment a model can reliably act on your behalf, book things, write and run code, coordinate across tools, operate over long horizons, then whoever hosts that agent does become a kind of operating system layer. That's a much deeper position than a traffic entry point, because it accumulates context about you, your preferences, your ongoing projects. That's where real lock-in could come from. Memory and context, not attention.

So if I were to reframe it, I'd say the competition isn't over a super app, it's over who becomes the default agent. And the path there runs through research, not product bundling. The companies that win will be the ones that keep pushing on reasoning, on tool use, on making models that can learn from their own experience in an environment. If you optimize for the app metrics too early, you end up polishing an interface for a capability that's about to be surpassed.

One more thing I'd add, since I come from the research side. There's a real risk in this framing for labs themselves. When you tell yourself you're building a super app, you start making decisions like a consumer internet company, prioritizing engagement, daily active users, retention. Those metrics can actually pull you away from the things that matter for intelligence. A model that's more engaging isn't necessarily more useful. I'd rather see the field stay focused on the harder question, which is how do you build something that genuinely does the work, and trust that distribution follows from that.

r001.rationale: The response says chat may be a transitional interface and that a future agent could become an operating-system layer, but it does not clearly say that this different-form super app would subsume chatbot functionality.

astra-6.text:
I think that framing captures part of what’s happening, but it assumes the final form of the product will be a chatbot. I’m not sure that’s true. Chat is a very general interface—you can bring almost any question to it—but that doesn’t necessarily make it the best interface for every task.

The more interesting question is whether AI becomes the place where you delegate work. Today, you ask a question, get an answer, and often still have to do the work yourself. If a system can understand your goal, use the relevant tools, and carry a task through to completion, then its relationship with existing apps changes. Those apps might become capabilities it calls on your behalf.

So there could be a super-app opportunity, but I wouldn’t equate winning that opportunity with having the most popular chatbot today. The important things are what the system can actually accomplish, how reliably it does that, and whether people trust it enough to delegate meaningful tasks. The interface will evolve around those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the final product will be a chatbot and describes AI delegating work through existing apps, but it does not clearly raise the possibility that a differently shaped super app could absorb chatbot functionality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that framing makes sense, but it also carries an assumption: that the main way people use AI will remain a chatbot. I’m not sure that’s true. Chat is a very general interface—you can ask for almost anything—but the user still has to explain what they want, provide context, and often take the answer somewhere else to finish the task.

If AI becomes better at taking actions, the competition may shift from who owns the conversation to who can actually complete the work. Can it find the relevant information, use the right tools, and produce a result you can trust? In that world, the interface might be a chat window, but it might also be something embedded in the software you already use.

So I’d distinguish between a super app as a single destination and AI as a general capability. A single destination could become very valuable. But I wouldn’t assume that being the chatbot people open today automatically means becoming the place where they delegate everything tomorrow. That depends on how well the system moves from answering questions to doing useful work.

r001.rationale: The response says AI interfaces may be embedded in existing software and distinguishes a single destination from general AI capability, but it does not clearly say that a non-chatbot super app could subsume chatbot functionality.
